module.title: Identity, authorization and audit
module.summary: Tell people from workloads, choose OAuth U2M, M2M or workload identity federation, keep secrets out of code, predict row filters, column masks and attribute-based policies, and use audit rows as evidence in a narrow, tested access review.
objectives: Identify who authenticated, whose permissions applied and where a request failed, for users, service principals and groups.
Choose OAuth U2M, OAuth M2M, workload identity federation or a secret scope for a given caller, and explain the token exposure mistakes each avoids.
Produce a threat and access review with a narrow permission plan, row and column controls, a must-fail test matrix, separated duties and an audit-based incident sequence.

scenarios.title: Threat and access review after Cinderline's leaked token
scenarios.context: Fictional Cinderline Components found a data engineer's personal access token in a notebook committed to its quality-jobs repository. The nightly ingest job runs as that engineer because nobody set its run-as identity; the supplier SFTP password sits in a secret scope readable by all workspace users; a supplier-portal prototype uses a quality lead's token with SELECT on the whole quality catalog; inspector emails are unmasked. Identities come from the company's identity provider through SCIM. The status of attribute-based policies for Cinderline's region is unconfirmed.
scenarios.task: Write a threat and access review for the security owner: containment and an evidence plan for the leaked token, redesigned identities and authentication for the ingest job, the CI deploy and the portal, a narrow permission plan, secret-scope ACLs, row filter and column mask decisions, a test matrix with must-fail rows, the separation of duties for applying it, and an explicit list of unknowns.
requirements: Contain the leaked token before any analysis and bound the evidence with an exposure window and audit queries.
Give every workload its own service principal with a named authentication method, leaving no personal or shared token in automation.
Grant to groups on the lowest securables that work, with a test matrix holding at least as many must-fail rows as must-succeed rows.
Separate request, approval, application and audit; never use administrator rights or ALL PRIVILEGES as a fix; claim no compliance certification.
scenarios.model:
### Containment
Revoke the token at once (the engineer or a workspace admin) and record the time. The exposure window runs from the commit to the revocation. Security queries system.access.audit for the engineer's identity inside the window and saves the result with the query time; the platform owner lists everything the engineer could reach, and every secret the engineer could read is rotated, starting with the SFTP password.

### Identities
Ingest job: run-as sp-nightly-ingest, a member of ingest-jobs. CI deploy: sp-ci-deploy through workload identity federation limited to the main branch. Portal: sp-supplier-portal through federation, or M2M with a secret held in the portal platform's store. Only release managers hold the servicePrincipal user role on each principal.

### Permission plan
ingest-jobs: MODIFY on quality.raw.deliveries with USE on its parents, and READ on scope supplier-sftp; users is removed from that ACL and MANAGE stays with quality-platform-owners. supplier-portal: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on quality.shared.supplier_rejections only, with a row filter for S-17 and a mask on inspector_email. Analysts keep reads through quality-analysts; direct user grants are removed.

### Test matrix (excerpt)
Portal reads supplier_rejections: allow. Portal reads inspections: deny. Portal writes supplier_rejections: deny. Portal rows for S-22: zero. An analyst reads scope supplier-sftp: deny. The engineer's personal MODIFY on raw deliveries: deny.

### Duties and unknowns
The quality lead requests, the schema owner approves, a platform administrator applies, and security reviews the audit rows and the matrix output. Unknown: attribute-based policy status in the region, audit delivery delay for the evidence, and whether the token was used from an unfamiliar address, pending the audit query.
scenarios.reasoning: The model contains before it analyses, replaces people and shared tokens with workload identities, keeps every grant narrow and group-based, proves narrowness with must-fail tests, and states unknowns instead of promising features or compliance.

rubric.weak: Replaces the token without revoking it, or reads audit logs before revoking.
rubric.partial: Revokes the token but gives no exposure window or saves no query evidence.
rubric.strong: Revokes first, fixes the window, queries audit rows inside it, lists the reach and rotates readable secrets.

rubric.weak: Keeps personal or shared tokens in automation.
rubric.partial: Introduces service principals but leaves their authentication unnamed or uses long-lived tokens.
rubric.strong: Each workload has its own service principal with M2M or federation, and run-as roles are limited to the deployers.

rubric.weak: Grants catalog-wide SELECT, MANAGE or admin membership to clear errors.
rubric.partial: Narrow grants, but no must-fail tests, or tests run as an administrator.
rubric.strong: Group grants on the lowest securables, filters and masks where needed, and a matrix with must-fail rows run as the real principals.

rubric.weak: One person requests, approves and applies, and the design is called compliant.
rubric.partial: Names an approver but omits audit review of the change or the unknowns.
rubric.strong: Four separate duties, audit review of the change, and explicit unknowns such as feature status and delivery delay.

disclosures.question: Was the leaked token used after it was committed?
disclosures.response: Unknown until security runs the audit query for the window; the token list's last-used day is the first signal, accurate only to one day.

disclosures.question: Can the supplier's platform issue identity tokens for federation?
disclosures.response: Its platform team says it can issue OIDC tokens, but the issuer and subject format are not confirmed, so the plan keeps M2M with a rotated secret as the fallback.

claims.description: Users are identities for people, represented by email addresses; service principals are identities for jobs, automated tools, scripts, apps and CI/CD platforms; Databricks recommends running production jobs as service principals so interactive users need no write, delete or modify privileges in production; Databricks-managed service principals exist on every cloud and reach only Databricks.

Groups can contain users, service principals and other groups; members inherit the permissions assigned to their group; assigning workspace access and Unity Catalog access-control policies to groups rather than individual users is documented best practice; account principals are assigned to a workspace with USER or ADMIN permission and receive workspace entitlements separately.

Databricks recommends SCIM provisioning to sync users and groups from the identity provider into the Databricks account, and terminating a user in the identity provider removes the user from the account; with identity federation enabled, user attributes are maintained through the account-level SCIM APIs rather than the workspace SCIM APIs.
claims.context: Provisioning and identity federation; connector specifics vary by identity provider.

claims.description: OAuth user-to-machine sign-in in the SDK's external-browser strategy runs an authorization-code flow with a PKCE challenge through the browser and a localhost redirect, requests offline_access for a refresh token and caches the tokens locally; after databricks auth login, tools can reuse the CLI profile's cached OAuth token, and every call acts as the signed-in user.
claims.context: Client behaviour of the SDK and CLI; server-side token lifetimes not stated.

claims.description: OAuth machine-to-machine authentication presents a service principal's client ID (its application ID) and an OAuth secret with the client-credentials grant at the Databricks token endpoint, discovered from /oidc/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server; the SDK requests the all-apis scope by default, sends the bearer token on each request and refreshes it before expiry.
claims.context: OAuth M2M on account and workspace APIs, all clouds.

claims.description: Service principal OAuth secrets are managed by administrators and used to obtain OAuth access tokens for account and workspace APIs; without an explicit lifetime a secret lasts 730 days, and each secret reports its creation time, expiry time and status.
claims.context: Default lifetime as documented by the provider at v1.133.0.

claims.description: Workload identity federation lets workloads outside Databricks authenticate as a service principal by exchanging a token issued by their own runtime, with no Databricks secret; a service principal federation policy names the accepted issuer and the permitted subject, audiences default to the Databricks account ID, and Databricks strongly recommends it over OAuth client secrets or personal access tokens whenever possible; account federation policies extend token federation to users and service principals and are typically combined with SCIM.
claims.context: Federation policies at account level; GA badge on the provider resources at v1.133.0.

claims.description: Databricks strongly recommends OAuth instead of personal access tokens for user authentication; personal access tokens carry a lifetime set at creation; the right to use tokens is itself a permission (CAN_USE on the tokens object); on-behalf-of tokens for service principals exist on AWS and Google Cloud but OAuth is generally preferred; administrators can list and delete other users' tokens, and token records carry creation time, expiry time and an approximate last-used day.

Secret scope ACLs grant READ (read and list), WRITE (read and write) or MANAGE (also change the ACL) to users, groups or service principals; secret values are read only from within a command on a cluster, with the permission of whoever runs the command; values can be referenced as {{secrets/scope/key}} in Spark configuration and environment variables; Databricks redacts secret values shown in notebooks where it can but cannot prevent a permitted user from reading a secret.

A job runs as its run-as identity and, when none is set, as the user who created it; making a service principal the run-as identity requires the servicePrincipal user role, account rule sets separate the service principal Manager and User roles, and job permissions separately control who can view, manage, trigger or cancel a job.

Row filters and column masks are SQL functions attached to a table and evaluated at query time: a row filter, attached with SET ROW FILTER ... ON (columns), receives table columns and returns whether a row is visible, and a column mask, attached with ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK, receives the masked column, with optional other columns, and returns the value to show, its first argument and return type matching the column; a query that meets them returns fewer rows or masked values rather than an error.
claims.context: Unity Catalog tables; supported compute and runtimes vary.

claims.description: Unity Catalog attribute-based access control policies are defined on a catalog, schema or table and apply to it and its descendants; they match tables and columns through conditions on governance tags and the user identity, apply a row filter or column mask function, name the principals they apply to and those excepted, and require MANAGE on the securable; the provider's page for the policy resource carried a GA badge when read on 2026-09-23.
claims.context: Status, supported compute and regions to be verified on the product page.

claims.description: The audit log system table system.access.audit records account and workspace events with event time, workspace, service and action names, the acting identity, request parameters, source IP address, user agent and response; system schemas, including access, are enabled by an account admin; on AWS, audit logs can also be delivered as JSON files to the account's S3 bucket, available within 15 minutes of activation, with new files every few minutes and occasional later arrivals.
claims.context: System tables and log delivery; coverage and delay change, and the system-table column names were not re-read in this build.

claims.description: Account rule sets on a service principal grant roles/servicePrincipal.manager to manage it and roles/servicePrincipal.user to use it; making a service principal a job's run-as identity requires the servicePrincipal user role; the provider manages rule sets authoritatively, overwriting unmanaged rules of the same type.

A service principal OAuth secret takes an optional lifetime in seconds and otherwise lasts 730 days; each secret exposes create_time, expire_time and a status such as ACTIVE; secrets can be listed per service principal and recreated for rotation.
claims.context: Default lifetime as documented by the provider at v1.133.0.

claims.description: Permission to use tokens is granted as CAN_USE on the tokens authorization object, and declaring it overwrites existing groups' token permissions unless they are included; administrators can list every token, list one user's tokens and delete tokens for other users; token records show the creator, expiry and an approximate last-used day.
claims.context: Workspace token permissions and token management.

claims.description: System tables are a Databricks-hosted store of the account's operational data that an account admin must enable schema by schema; enablement is identified per metastore and schema; some schemas are enabled automatically and some cannot be disabled; system schemas live in the system catalog.

concepts.definition: Any identity Databricks can authenticate or authorize: a user for a person, a service principal for a workload, or a group that collects them.
SCIM copies users and groups from the identity provider into the Databricks account; identity federation assigns those account identities to workspaces.
OAuth user-to-machine sign-in lets a tool act as a signed-in person; OAuth machine-to-machine lets a service principal trade its secret for an access token.
A credential that authenticates whoever presents it as the principal it was issued to, until it expires or is revoked.
A named store of secret values whose READ, WRITE and MANAGE entries decide who may read, change or administer them at run time.
The principal whose privileges are checked for a request: the user for interactive work, the run-as identity for a job.

concepts.term: row filters, column masks and ABAC
concepts.definition: Query-time functions that remove rows or replace column values for the calling principal, attached per table or through attribute-based policies on tagged data.
Rows in the audit log system table that tie an identity to an action, a time, a source address and a response, used to reconstruct what happened.
A permission plan at the narrowest working scope, a test matrix with must-fail rows, and separate people to request, approve, apply and audit it.
